story: In 2022, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva beat Jair Bolsonaro by less than two points. A week after Lula took office, Bolsonaro's supporters stormed Congress, the Supreme Court and the presidential palace in Brasília, and in 2025 Bolsonaro was convicted of plotting a coup and sentenced to 27 years in prison. That is the backdrop for 2026: Brazil is choosing between the same two camps, with the father replaced by his son.

On 4 October, Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, 45, Jair's eldest son, beat the polls and finished first with 47.45 percent; Lula, now 80, took 44.66 percent (Reuters via Emirates 24/7). Nearly every pre-election survey had Lula ahead in the first round. Lula admitted he had expected to win outright; Flávio called the result "the beginning of the end" of the Workers' Party era and quickly picked up endorsements from defeated right-wing governors Ronaldo Caiado and Romeu Zema (Blueprint). The right also did well in congressional races, which could give Flávio a working base if he wins (Al Jazeera). Lula has accused Trump of trying to tilt the race. Voters' top worries are crime, corruption and the cost of living. The runoff is on 25 October, and the question is whether Brazil hands power back to the family whose last term ended with a mob in the capital.
briefing.power: A federal presidential republic. The president is directly elected for four years with one consecutive re-election, needing a majority, with a runoff if no one passes 50 percent. Congress has two chambers and is highly fragmented, so presidents govern through coalitions with dozens of parties; the 26 states and federal district have their own governors.
briefing.holders: President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT), in office since 2023, facing a runoff on 25 October.
